items.headline: Boston Aims to Tackle 100-year Flood Risks with $10 Billion in Infrastructure Projects
items.facts: Boston and the US Army Corps of Engineers released a feasibility study proposing 20 infrastructure projects to protect the city from future flooding.

framing.narrativeTitle: Boston and the Corps Plot the Flood Shield
framing.publicBrief: Boston and the US Army Corps of Engineers unveil a joint study outlining twenty projects aimed at shielding the city from a century‑old flood threat. The plan calls for billions in upgrades to levees, storm‑drain tunnels, and coastal barriers. Both parties must decide whether to move forward together or each pursue separate, smaller fixes, knowing the city’s future safety hangs in the balance.

roleFlavor.hunter: You represent Boston’s municipal leaders, holding the city’s budget and public trust, watching the Corps’ engineering assessments and the political pressure from residents.

STAG.label: FULL COORDINATION
STAG.meaning: Boston and the Corps commit to the full twenty‑project plan together
STAG.outcome: All projects are built as designed, delivering the strongest flood defenses for the city

HARE.label: SEPARATE ACTIONS
HARE.meaning: Boston pursues a reduced set of projects while the Corps scales back its involvement
HARE.outcome: Only a portion of the defenses are completed, leaving gaps in protection

howItWorks: Boston controls funding approvals and local permits
The Corps provides engineering designs and federal support
Both must agree on the scope to unlock construction contracts
If either side pulls back, the unfinished projects stall
missionCopy.choicePrompt: How will Boston proceed with the flood‑protection plan?

outcomes.COOPERATIVE: Boston and the Corps finish all twenty projects, dramatically lowering flood risk
outcomes.BETRAYAL: Boston goes it alone, completing only a few works while the Corps withdraws, leaving the city vulnerable
outcomes.MIXED: Boston scales back and the Corps reduces its role, resulting in partial protection and ongoing debate

framing.publicBrief: Boston and the US Army Corps of Engineers have released a feasibility study proposing 20 infrastructure projects to protect the city from future flooding. The document outlines specific upgrades to levees, storm-drain tunnels, and coastal barriers. Both parties must now determine how to prioritize these initiatives. The success of the plan depends on identifying which of the 20 proposals offers the most robust protection against a 100-year flood event, requiring a shared understanding of the city's most critical vulnerabilities.

roleFlavor.guesser: You are a planner reviewing the 20 proposed infrastructure projects. Your goal is to identify the single project that offers the best balance of cost and protection, assuming other planners are doing

howItWorks: Boston and the US Army Corps of Engineers have proposed 20 distinct infrastructure projects.
Each planner must select the single project they believe offers the most effective flood protection.
The goal is not to pick the absolute best project, but to guess which project most other planners will select.
Success comes from aligning your choice with the collective judgment of the group.
missionCopy.choicePrompt: Which project will the majority choose?

outcomes.COOPERATIVE: The group converges on a single priority project.
outcomes.BETRAYAL: Choices are scattered; no clear consensus emerges.
outcomes.MIXED: Partial agreement, but significant disagreement remains.

items.headline: ‘Can’t enjoy your pint’: Wetherspoons customers welcome ban on loud phones
items.facts: Wetherspoons owner Tim Martin banned loud phones and music in pubs. Customers Gary and Mark supported the ban, agreeing rude customers should be barred.

framing.publicBrief: Tim Martin, owner of Wetherspoons, has banned loud phones and music in his pubs. Patrons Gary and Mark back the ban, arguing that rude customers should be barred. The decision to enforce or lift the ban will shape the night’s atmosphere.

roleFlavor.hunter: You are Tim Martin, the pub owner deciding whether to enforce the new ban.

STAG.label: Enforce Ban
STAG.meaning: Apply the loud‑phone and music ban in the pub
STAG.outcome: Patrons enjoy a quiet evening, and Gary and Mark applaud the decision.

HARE.label: Lift Ban
HARE.meaning: Allow loud phones and music again
HARE.outcome: Noise returns, some patrons leave, while others remain.

howItWorks: Tim must decide whether to keep the ban in place or allow loud phones again.
Patrons Gary and Mark support the ban, while other customers may disagree.
The outcome depends on Tim’s choice alone; the other patrons cannot influence the rule.
missionCopy.choicePrompt: Choose how to handle noisy phones tonight

outcomes.MIXED: Mixed reactions, some leave, some stay
